newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hijacker used kitchen knife, security chief says.
newsitem.headline: Hijacker used kitchen knife, security chief says.

text.p: A Bosnian refugee who hijacked a plane flying from Berlin to Vienna wielded a short kitchen knife of the sort that passengers are normally permitted to take on board, Berlin airport security said on Wednesday.

The 39-year-old hijacker was disarmed by police commandos at Berlin's Tegel airport on Tuesday about two hours after he had put a knife to the throat of the Austrian Airlines pilot and ordered the plane to return to Berlin.
"The blade of the kitchen knife was only nine centimetres (3-1/2 inches) long," Reinhard Ottens, director for the Securitas airport security firm at Tegel airport, said in a statement.
"According to existing security regulations, such a knife may be brought on board. The federal border police have confirmed that our staff was not at fault."
Berlin police confirmed the length of the knife was nine cm. Earlier reports had put the knife's length at anywhere between 25 cm (10 inches) and 50 cm.

Although the hijacker gave police a full confession on Wednesday, it was still unclear how he smuggled the knife and a two batons -- 43 cm (17 inches) long and five cm (two inches) thick -- on to the plane.
The hijacker was also carrying about 50 cigarette lighters with him, police said.
He had demanded permission to stay and work in Germany.
The standoff ended without bloodshed when police secretly entered a rear door of the plane and pushed the hijacker out of an open door in the front.
He fell about seven metres (20 feet) to the tarmac where he was quickly overpowered and detained. None of the passengers or crew was hurt.
The Bosnian, who arrived in Germany in 1992, had a residence permit which expired on December 2. Authorities in Rostock, where he lived, had ordered him to leave Germany before January 15.

The leader of the Berlin police union criticised the airport management for hiring private firms for airport security. Eberhard Schoenberg, Berlin chairman of the police union GdP, said private companies were inadequate for the task.

"Saving costs cannot be the overriding aim of airport security," Schoenberg said. "It is irreponsible to privatise these tasks and hand them over to the lowest bidder. It is a scandal that a baton and knife can be smuggled on board."
Security at the west Berlin airport has been thorough since the Cold War era. It includes body searches of all passengers boarding aircraft.
Securitas, which has guarded airports in Munich for many years, took over security at Tegel on January 1, outbidding five competitors for the contract.
The Interior Ministry in Bonn said security at Tegel had not deteriorated with the change. "The security standard is just as high now, if not higher, as it was before," a spokesman said.
About 320,000 Bosnian refugees live in Germany. Several German states recently began the forced repatration of Bosnians now that the 43-month-long war there has ended.
The Bosnian, who was in police custody, was due to appear in court late on Wednesday to face likely charges of kidnapping and air piracy. He could face up to 15 years in jail if convicted.
